adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:33 — [P2/75] `return cls(**input_dict)` accepts `integration_id` without runtime normalization while `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` compares it strictly, so a valid task payload encoded with `"integration_id": "123"` is accepted but fails to suppress the originating integration and echoes the assignment back to its source; the annotation is not a runtime guard and therefore does not rebut the queue-boundary format drift.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that passing a string '123' instead of int 123 for integration_id would cause the comparison to fail. However, looking at the diff: 1) The `to_dict()` method uses `asdict()` which preserves the original int type from the dataclass field `integration_id: int`. 2) The `from_dict()` method uses `cls(**input_dict)` which would pass the value directly to the dataclass constructor. 3) The dataclass has `integration_id: int` type annotation, but Python dataclasses don't enforce types at runtime - they accept whatever is passed. 4) However, the actual serialization path shown in the diff (`assignment_source.to_dict()`) preserves the int type since it comes from `integration.id` which is an integer. The finding assumes a scenario where the payload contains a string, but the diff shows the serialization always uses the integer from `integration.id`. This is a theoretical concern not grounded in the actual code paths shown.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:441 — [P1/75] `sync_status_inbound_task.apply_async(kwargs={"integration_id": self.model.id, "organization_id": self.organization_id, "issue_key": issue_key, "data": data})` drops the originating integration while the diff adds source-aware outbound status synchronization, so an inbound status update is sent back to its source and recreates the synchronization cycle that this change is intended to stop.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that while the diff adds AssignmentSource tracking for outbound assignee sync (sync_assignee_outbound), the sync_status_inbound_task.apply_async call at line 441 (referenced in the finding) does not pass the integration source information. Looking at the diff, sync_status_outbound method signature was updated to accept assignment_source parameter, but the inbound status sync task doesn't propagate this information. This means status updates coming from an integration would still be sent back to that same integration, creating a sync cycle. The diff shows the pattern was implemented for assignee sync but not consistently applied to status sync.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:31 — [P1/75] `return cls(**input_dict)` accepts wrong-typed `integration_id` values while `except (ValueError, TypeError): return None` silently downgrades forward-versioned payloads to an originless assignment, so line 56's source guard misses the originating integration and the task reports success after echoing the assignment back into the same system.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that `cls(**input_dict)` accepts wrong-typed `integration_id` values, but looking at the dataclass definition, `integration_id: int` is a type hint, not a runtime validator. Python dataclasses don't enforce types at runtime by default. The `from_dict` method catches ValueError and TypeError which would occur if required fields are missing or if the constructor fails. The claim about 'forward-versioned payloads' being silently downgraded is speculative - the code handles malformed input by returning None, which is reasonable defensive coding. The finding mischaracterizes the behavior and the actual risk is not demonstrated by the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/services/assignment_source.py:18 — [P2/100 advisory] `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` evaluates once at module import, so every subsequently constructed source that omits `queued` receives the worker-start timestamp and any age-based observability, expiry, or retry logic classifies fresh assignments as old.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` as a default argument in a dataclass field at line 18 of assignment_source.py. In Python, default argument values are evaluated once at function/class definition time, not at each call. This means `timezone.now()` is called once when the module is imported, and all AssignmentSource instances created without explicitly passing `queued` will share that same timestamp from module import time. This is a well-known Python gotcha with mutable/time-based defaults. The finding correctly identifies this as a bug that would cause incorrect timestamps.

adjudication_records.issue_text: src/sentry/integrations/mixins/issues.py:411 — [P3/100] The unrelated API expansion `def sync_status_outbound(... assignment_source: AssignmentSource | None = None, ...)` forces every status-sync provider to carry an assignment-specific parameter that no status call site supplies, adding dead contract surface outside the assignee-cycle change.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that adding assignment_source to sync_status_outbound is 'unrelated' and 'dead contract surface'. However, looking at the diff context and the comment on lines 384-387, the purpose is to 'prevent sync-cycles from occurring' - this applies to both assignee AND status syncing. The parameter is being added to the abstract method signature as part of a consistent pattern to prevent sync cycles across all sync operations, not just assignee sync. The finding mischaracterizes this as 'dead' when it's actually part of the same cycle-prevention architecture being implemented.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:218 — [P1/100] The only cycle-prevention test injects `assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration),` directly into `GroupAssignee.objects.assign`, so deleting source propagation from `sync_group_assignee_inbound` leaves the test green while real inbound assignments and deassignments echo back to their origin integration.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. Looking at the diff, `sync_group_assignee_inbound` in `src/sentry/integrations/utils/sync.py` does pass `assignment_source=AssignmentSource.from_integration(integration)` to both `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` and `GroupAssignee.objects.deassign`. However, the test `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` directly calls `GroupAssignee.objects.assign` with the assignment_source parameter, rather than testing through `sync_group_assignee_inbound`. This means the test doesn't verify the actual inbound sync flow that would occur in production. While the code in `sync_group_assignee_inbound` appears correct, there's no test that exercises the full inbound-to-outbound cycle prevention path through `sync_group_assignee_inbound`. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for newly added logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/models/test_groupassignee.py:221 — [P1/75] The sole source-bearing case asserts only `mock_sync_assignee_outbound.assert_not_called()` for one matching integration, so an implementation that suppresses every non-null assignment source passes while assignments fail to propagate to other linked integrations.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap. The test at line 221 only verifies that when assignment_source matches the integration, sync is not called. However, there's no test verifying that when a group is linked to multiple integrations, an assignment from one integration still propagates to OTHER linked integrations. The implementation in should_sync() checks if sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id, which should allow propagation to different integrations, but this behavior is not tested. This is a legitimate test coverage concern for the new cycle-prevention logic.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:14 — [P1/100] The test labeled invalid data supplies only `"foo": "bar",`, so `AssignmentSource.from_dict` accepting `{"source_name": "x", "integration_id": "123"}` remains undetected and the string ID fails the integer equality guard, re-enabling a same-integration sync cycle.

adjudication.rationale: The finding claims that passing a string ID like '123' instead of integer 123 would bypass the equality guard. However, looking at the diff, the `from_dict` method in AssignmentSource uses `cls(**input_dict)` which would pass the values directly to the dataclass constructor. The dataclass has `integration_id: int` type annotation, but Python dataclasses don't enforce types at runtime - they just accept whatever is passed. The equality check `sync_source.integration_id == self.org_integration.integration_id` would indeed fail if one is string and one is int, but this is not a realistic scenario. The `from_dict` is called with data that comes from `to_dict()` which uses `asdict()` on a properly constructed AssignmentSource, so the integration_id would always be an int. The test coverage concern is valid but the specific attack vector described (string ID causing sync cycle) is not a realistic bug.

adjudication_records.issue_text: tests/sentry/integrations/services/test_assignment_source.py:36 — [Advisory/P2/100] The assertion `assert result.get("queued") is not None` passes when every `AssignmentSource` shares the import-time default timestamp, so despite `queued` being unused today the first age-based consumer will classify fresh work using a stale queue time.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a real bug in the AssignmentSource dataclass. Looking at line 17 of assignment_source.py: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` - this sets the default value at class definition time (import time), not at instance creation time. This means all instances that don't explicitly pass a `queued` parameter will share the same timestamp from when the module was imported. The test at line 36 only checks `is not None` which passes regardless of this bug. This is a genuine defect that would cause incorrect timestamps for any time-based logic using the `queued` field.
